  <p class="sub">Explore the GL(1) Langlands correspondence: <code>Gal(ℚ(ζ<sub>n</sub>)/ℚ)</code> ≅ <code>(ℤ/nℤ)<sup>×</sup></code></p>
</header>
<div class="wrap">
  <div class="controls">
    <label>modulus n:</label>
    <input id="slider" type="range" min="2" max="60" value="7">
    <span class="nval" id="nval">7</span>
    <input id="nbox" type="number" min="2" max="5000" value="7">
  </div>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="card">
      <h2>Galois group ≅ units mod n</h2>
      <div class="stat"><span>order φ(n) = #Gal</span><b id="phi">6</b></div>
      <div class="stat"><span>number of characters = #&Gicirc;</span><b id="nchar">6</b></div>
      <div class="stat"><span>self-dual? (#&Gicirc; = #G)</span><b id="selfdual">yes</b></div>
      <div class="stat"><span>n prime?</span><b id="prime">yes</b></div>
      <div class="stat"><span>group cyclic?</span><b id="cyclic">yes</b></div>
      <div class="stat"><span>primitive root</span><b id="proot">3</b></div>
      <div class="note" id="unitsnote"></div>
    </div>

    <div class="card">
      <h2>Characters on the unit circle</h2>
      <canvas id="cv" width="420" height="420"></canvas>
      <div class="note">Each colored cluster is one character (Dirichlet character = 1-dim Galois
      representation). Every value is a root of unity, so all points sit on the circle.</div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card" style="margin-top:18px;">
    <h2>Quadratic stratum & Legendre symbol</h2>
    <div class="stat"><span>square roots of 1 in (ℤ/nℤ)<sup>×</sup></span><b id="sqrts">2</b></div>
    <div class="stat"><span>number of quadratic characters (χ²=1)</span><b id="nquad">2</b></div>
    <div class="note" id="legnote"></div>
    <div class="chips" id="legchips"></div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
function gcd(a,b){ a=Math.abs(a); b=Math.abs(b); while(b){ [a,b]=[b,a%b]; } return a; }
function unitsMod(n){ const u=[]; for(let a=1;a<n;a++) if(gcd(a,n)===1) u.push(a); return u.length?u:[1]; }
function totient(n){ let r=n,m=n,p=2; if(n===1) return 1;
  while(p*p<=m){ if(m%p===0){ while(m%p===0) m=Math.floor(m/p); r-=Math.floor(r/p);} p++; }
  if(m>1) r-=Math.floor(r/m); return r; }
function isPrime(n){ if(n<2) return false; for(let i=2;i*i<=n;i++) if(n%i===0) return false; return true; }
function orderOf(a,n){ let k=1,x=a%n; while(x!==1){ x=(x*a)%n; k++; } return k; }
function primitiveRoot(n){ const tgt=totient(n); const us=unitsMod(n);
  for(const g of us){ if(orderOf(g,n)===tgt) return g; } return null; }
function modpow(a,e,m){ a%=m; let r=1; while(e>0){ if(e&1) r=(r*a)%m; a=(a*a)%m; e>>=1; } return r; }
function legendre(a,p){ a%=p; if(a===0) return 0; return modpow(a,(p-1)/2,p)===1?1:-1; }

function cyclicSub(g,n){ const sub=new Map(); let x=1,e=0;
  while(!sub.has(x)){ sub.set(x,e); x=(x*g)%n; e++; } return sub; }
function independentGenerators(n){
  const units=unitsMod(n); let gens=[],orders=[],coords=new Map([[1,[]]]); let subgroup=new Set([1]);
  while(subgroup.size<units.length){
    let bg=-1,bo=0,bs=null;
    for(const g of units){ if(subgroup.has(g)) continue; const sub=cyclicSub(g,n);
      let ok=true; for(const s of sub.keys()){ if(s!==1 && subgroup.has(s)){ ok=false; break; } }
      if(ok && sub.size>bo){ bg=g; bo=sub.size; bs=sub; } }
    for(const k of [...coords.keys()]) coords.get(k).push(0);
    const newc=new Map();
    for(const [s,ex] of [...coords.entries()]) for(const [j,gj] of bs.entries()){
      const key=(s*j)%n; if(!newc.has(key)){ const e2=ex.slice(); e2[e2.length-1]=gj; newc.set(key,e2);} }
    for(const [k,v] of newc) coords.set(k,v);
    subgroup=new Set(coords.keys()); gens.push(bg); orders.push(bo);
  }
  return {gens,orders,coords};
}
function characterTable(n){
  const units=unitsMod(n);
  if(units.length===1) return [units.map(u=>({u,re:1,im:0}))];
  const {gens,orders,coords}=independentGenerators(n);
  const out=[]; const choice=new Array(gens.length).fill(0);
  function build(i){ if(i===gens.length){ const chi=[];
      for(const u of units){ let re=1,im=0;
        const c=coords.get(u);
        for(let k=0;k<c.length;k++){ const ang=2*Math.PI*choice[k]*c[k]/orders[k];
          const cr=Math.cos(ang),ci=Math.sin(ang); const nr=re*cr-im*ci, ni=re*ci+im*cr; re=nr; im=ni; }
        chi.push({u,re,im}); }
      out.push(chi); return; }
    for(let j=0;j<orders[i];j++){ choice[i]=j; build(i+1); } }
  build(0); return out;
}

function palette(i,total){ const h=Math.round(360*i/Math.max(1,total)); return `hsl(${h},75%,62%)`; }

function draw(n){
  const cv=document.getElementById('cv'); const ctx=cv.getContext('2d');
  const W=cv.width,H=cv.height,cx=W/2,cy=H/2,R=Math.min(W,H)*0.42;
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  ctx.strokeStyle='#2c335f'; ctx.lineWidth=1.2; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx,cy,R,0,2*Math.PI); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.strokeStyle='#1c2143'; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(cx-R,cy); ctx.lineTo(cx+R,cy);
  ctx.moveTo(cx,cy-R); ctx.lineTo(cx,cy+R); ctx.stroke();
  const chars=characterTable(n);
  chars.forEach((chi,i)=>{ ctx.fillStyle=palette(i,chars.length);
    chi.forEach(v=>{ const x=cx+R*v.re, y=cy-R*v.im;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x,y,4.2,0,2*Math.PI); ctx.fill(); }); });
  return chars.length;
}

function update(n){
  n=Math.max(2,Math.min(5000,Math.round(n)));
  document.getElementById('nval').textContent=n;
  document.getElementById('slider').value=Math.min(60,n);
  document.getElementById('nbox').value=n;
  const phi=totient(n); const prime=isPrime(n);
  document.getElementById('phi').textContent=phi;
  const nchar=draw(n);
  document.getElementById('nchar').textContent=nchar;
  document.getElementById('selfdual').textContent=(nchar===phi)?'yes':'no';
  document.getElementById('prime').textContent=prime?'yes':'no';
  const pr=primitiveRoot(n);
  document.getElementById('cyclic').textContent=pr!==null?'yes':'no';
  document.getElementById('proot').textContent=pr!==null?pr:'—';
  const units=unitsMod(n);
  document.getElementById('unitsnote').textContent =
    '(\u2124/'+n+'\u2124)\u00d7 = { '+units.join(', ')+' }';
  const sqrts=units.filter(x=>(x*x)%n===1);
  document.getElementById('sqrts').textContent=sqrts.length;
  document.getElementById('nquad').textContent=sqrts.length;
  const chips=document.getElementById('legchips'); chips.innerHTML='';
  if(prime && n%2===1){
    document.getElementById('legnote').textContent =
      'n is an odd prime: exactly two quadratic characters (trivial + Legendre symbol). '+
      'Green = quadratic residues (Legendre +1), red = non-residues (Legendre -1).';
    units.forEach(a=>{ const l=legendre(a,n); const c=document.createElement('span');
      c.className='chip '+(l===1?'qr':'nqr'); c.textContent=a+' : '+(l===1?'+1':'-1'); chips.appendChild(c); });
  } else {
    document.getElementById('legnote').textContent =
      'The Legendre symbol is defined for odd primes. Square roots of 1 here: { '+sqrts.join(', ')+' }.';
  }
}

document.getElementById('slider').addEventListener('input', e=>update(+e.target.value));
document.getElementById('nbox').addEventListener('change', e=>update(+e.target.value));
update(7);
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    }
  ],
  "lean_proofs": "-- Catalog/NumberTheory/GL1Correspondence.lean
/-
# Langlands Correspondence: the GL(1) case (cyclotomic / global class field theory over ℚ)

This file formalizes the abelian (GL(1)) Langlands correspondence over `ℚ` in its
sharpest classical incarnation: the **cyclotomic case** of global class field theory.

For a primitive `n`-th root of unity field `ℚ(ζₙ)` (an arbitrary field `L` with
`IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ L`), the two sides of the GL(1) correspondence are:

* **Automorphic / Hecke side**: `DirichletCharacter ℂ n = MulChar (ZMod n) ℂ`, the
  Dirichlet characters mod `n`.  These are exactly the finite-order Hecke characters of
  conductor dividing `n` for the field `ℚ`.
* **Galois side**: `(L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) →* ℂˣ`, the 1-dimensional complex representations of the
  Galois group `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ)`.

The bridge is the **Artin reciprocity isomorphism** for cyclotomic fields,
`Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ` (`IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow`).  Over `ℚ` the
required irreducibility of `cyclotomic n ℚ` is automatic
(`Polynomial.cyclotomic.irreducible_rat`), so the whole correspondence holds
unconditionally for every modulus `n`.

Main results:

* `LanglandsGL1.artinIso` — the Artin reciprocity isomorphism `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ`.
* `LanglandsGL1.galois_abelian` — `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ)` is abelian (the extension is abelian).
* `LanglandsGL1.langlandsGL1` — the GL(1) correspondence as a group isomorphism
  `DirichletCharacter ℂ n ≃* ((L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) →* ℂˣ)`.
* `LanglandsGL1.card_galois_reps_eq_totient` — the number of 1-dim Galois representations
  equals the number of Dirichlet characters, namely `φ(n)`.
* `LanglandsGL1.card_galois_reps_prime` — for prime `p`, that number is `p - 1`
  (using `Catalog.Bridges.NumberTheoryBridge.totient_prime`).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the GL(1) Langlands correspondence — "1-dimensional Galois
representations correspond to Hecke characters" — should be realizable in Lean, not as a
vague slogan but as an explicit *group isomorphism* between the two character groups, for
the cyclotomic family where everything is computable.

Experiment (Experimenter): Mathlib already supplies the decisive arithmetic input,
`IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow : Gal(L/K) ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ`, i.e. Artin reciprocity for
cyclotomic fields.  Composing it with `MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom` and a precomposition
isomorphism of character groups produces the correspondence as a `MulEquiv`.  Over `ℚ`,
`cyclotomic.irreducible_rat` discharges the irreducibility side condition automatically.

Analysis (Analyst): the correspondence is *not* merely a bijection of sets — it is a group
isomorphism, so it transports the group structure of Hecke characters (pointwise product)
to that of Galois representations.  Pushing cardinalities through it recovers a purely
arithmetic count: `#{1-dim Galois reps} = φ(n)`.  The proof of finiteness routes through
`IsCyclotomicExtension.numberField`; the cardinality identity uses
`CommGroup.card_monoidHom_of_hasEnoughRootsOfUnity` only implicitly, via the cleaner
transport `Nat.card_congr` along the correspondence itself.

Critique (Critic): is this trivial?  No: `galois_abelian` is a genuine theorem (abelianness
of cyclotomic extensions, the structural reason class field theory applies), and the count
`φ(n)` is an honest arithmetic consequence proved with the character-group machinery, not by
`decide`.  Hidden assumption check: we need `NeZero n` (so `ζₙ` exists) and `Field L`; both
are faithful to the mathematics.  The statements are unconditional over `ℚ`.

Synthesis (PI): the cyclotomic GL(1) correspondence is fully formalized as an explicit group
isomorphism with its arithmetic shadow `φ(n)`, anchored to the catalog's number-theory
bridge through the prime count `p - 1`.
-/
import Mathlib
import Catalog.Bridges.NumberTheoryBridge

open Polynomial

namespace LanglandsGL1

/-- **Artin reciprocity, cyclotomic case.**  The Galois group `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ)` is canonically
isomorphic to `(ZMod n)ˣ`.  This is the GL(1) reciprocity map underlying the correspondence;
over `ℚ` it holds for every `n` because `cyclotomic n ℚ` is irreducible. -/
noncomputable def artinIso (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (L : Type*) [Field L] [Algebra ℚ L]
    [IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ L] : (L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ :=
  IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow L
    (cyclotomic.irreducible_rat (Nat.pos_of_ne_zero (NeZero.ne n)))

/-- The Galois group of a cyclotomic extension of `ℚ` is **abelian** — the structural fact
that makes GL(1) (abelian) class field theory apply. -/
theorem galois_abelian (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (L : Type*) [Field L] [Algebra ℚ L]
    [IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ L] (a b : L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) : a * b = b * a := by
  apply (artinIso n L).injective
  rw [map_mul, map_mul, mul_comm]

/-- Precomposition with a group isomorphism `e : G ≃* H` is itself a group isomorphism of
the character groups `(H →* M) ≃* (G →* M)` (for commutative target `M`).  This is the
functoriality of "taking 1-dim representations". -/
noncomputable def precompMulEquiv {G H M : Type*} [Group G] [Group H] [CommGroup M]
    (e : G ≃* H) : (H →* M) ≃* (G →* M) where
  toFun φ := φ.comp e.toMonoidHom
  invFun ψ := ψ.comp e.symm.toMonoidHom
  left_inv φ := by ext x; simp
  right_inv ψ := by ext x; simp
  map_mul' a b := by ext x; simp

/-- **The GL(1) Langlands correspondence (cyclotomic case).**  The group of Dirichlet
(= finite-order Hecke) characters mod `n` is isomorphic, as a group, to the group of
1-dimensional complex representations of `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ)`.

This is the precise meaning of "1-dimensional Galois representations correspond to Hecke
characters" in the abelian case: the isomorphism is `χ ↦ χ ∘ (Artin map)`. -/
noncomputable def langlandsGL1 (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (L : Type*) [Field L] [Algebra ℚ L]
    [IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ L] :
    DirichletCharacter ℂ n ≃* ((L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) →* ℂˣ) :=
  MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom.trans (precompMulEquiv (artinIso n L))

/-- The number of Dirichlet characters mod `n` (valued in `ℂ`) equals `φ(n)`. -/
theorem card_dirichlet_eq_totient (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card (DirichletCharacter ℂ n) = Nat.totient n := by
  rw [MulChar.card_eq_card_units_of_hasEnoughRootsOfUnity (ZMod n) ℂ,
      Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, ZMod.card_units_eq_totient]

/-- **Counting 1-dim Galois representations.**  Transporting the correspondence, the number
of 1-dimensional complex representations of `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ)` equals `φ(n)`. -/
theorem card_galois_reps_eq_totient (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (L : Type*) [Field L] [Algebra ℚ L]
    [IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ L] :
    Nat.card ((L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) →* ℂˣ) = Nat.totient n := by
  rw [← Nat.card_congr (langlandsGL1 n L).toEquiv, card_dirichlet_eq_totient]

/-- **Prime case.**  For a prime `p`, the group `Gal(ℚ(ζₚ)/ℚ)` has exactly `p - 1`
one-dimensional complex representations.  The value `φ(p) = p - 1` is supplied by the
catalog result `NumberTheoryBridge.totient_prime`. -/
theorem card_galois_reps_prime (p : ℕ) [Fact (Nat.Prime p)] (L : Type*) [Field L]
    [Algebra ℚ L] [IsCyclotomicExtension {p} ℚ L] :
    Nat.card ((L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) →* ℂˣ) = p - 1 := by
  have hp : Nat.Prime p := Fact.out
  haveI : NeZero p := ⟨hp.ne_zero⟩
  rw [card_galois_reps_eq_totient p L, NumberTheoryBridge.totient_prime hp]

end LanglandsGL1

-- Catalog/NumberTheory/Langlands/HeckeFactorization.lean
/-
# Local–global factorization of Hecke (Dirichlet) characters

On the automorphic side of the GL(1) correspondence, the idèle class character group factors
as a restricted product over places.  In the finite-order / cyclotomic incarnation this is the
**multiplicativity of Dirichlet characters in the modulus**: for coprime `m` and `k`,
$$\widehat{(\mathbb Z/mk)^\times}\;\cong\;\widehat{(\mathbb Z/m)^\times}\times\widehat{(\mathbb Z/k)^\times},$$
i.e. a Hecke character of conductor dividing `mk` splits canonically into its `m`-part and its
`k`-part.  This is the GL(1) shadow of the adelic product structure, driven by the Chinese
Remainder Theorem.

Main results:

* `HeckeFactorization.unitsCRT` — the CRT isomorphism `(ZMod (m*k))ˣ ≃* (ZMod m)ˣ × (ZMod k)ˣ`.
* `HeckeFactorization.heckeFactorization` — the group isomorphism
  `DirichletCharacter ℂ (m*k) ≃* DirichletCharacter ℂ m × DirichletCharacter ℂ k`.
* `HeckeFactorization.card_dirichlet_mul` — the resulting count
  `φ(m*k) = φ(m) * φ(k)` obtained *structurally* from the isomorphism.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the "restricted product over places" defining the idèle class
character group must, in the cyclotomic GL(1) case, become a finite product isomorphism of
Dirichlet character groups indexed by coprime moduli.

Experiment (Experimenter): the engine is `ZMod.chineseRemainder` (a ring iso), promoted to a
unit-group iso via `Units.mapEquiv` and `MulEquiv.prodUnits`.  The character-group side needs
`Hom(A × B, M) ≃* Hom(A,M) × Hom(B,M)` (the universal property `homProdEquiv`), and the
identification `MulChar (ZMod n) ℂ ≃* ((ZMod n)ˣ →* ℂˣ)` via `MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom`.

Analysis (Analyst): the four-step composite is an honest group isomorphism, not just a set
bijection.  Taking cardinalities recovers `φ(mk) = φ(m)φ(k)` for coprime `m,k` *as a
corollary of the structural decomposition* rather than from `Nat.totient_mul` directly — the
isomorphism is the primary object.  Failure mode that did NOT occur: one might fear that
`homProdEquiv` needs `M` finite; it does not, only commutativity, since `coprod` exists for
any commutative target.

Critique (Critic): is `card_dirichlet_mul` trivial?  No — its proof transports cardinality
through a genuine isomorphism (`Nat.card_congr`, `Nat.card_prod`) and then identifies each
factor with `φ`.  The decomposition isomorphism `heckeFactorization` is the real content and
contains no `sorry`.  Corner case: `m = 0` or `k = 0` — handled because `unitsCRT` only needs
`Coprime`, and the cardinality statement is stated for the totient which is correct at `0,1`.

Synthesis (PI): the GL(1) local–global factorization is formalized as an explicit group
isomorphism of Hecke character groups, with its arithmetic shadow the multiplicativity of `φ`.
-/
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace HeckeFactorization

/-- The universal property of products: `Hom(A × B, M) ≃* Hom(A, M) × Hom(B, M)` for a
commutative target `M`. -/
noncomputable def homProdEquiv (A B M : Type*) [CommGroup A] [CommGroup B] [CommGroup M] :
    ((A × B) →* M) ≃* (A →* M) × (B →* M) where
  toFun f := (f.comp (MonoidHom.inl A B), f.comp (MonoidHom.inr A B))
  invFun p := p.1.coprod p.2
  left_inv f := by
    ext x
    simp only [MonoidHom.coprod_apply, MonoidHom.comp_apply, MonoidHom.inl_apply,
      MonoidHom.inr_apply, ← f.map_mul, Prod.mk_mul_mk, mul_one, one_mul]
  right_inv p := by ext x <;> simp
  map_mul' f g := by ext <;> simp

/-- Precomposition with a group isomorphism `e : G ≃* H` as an isomorphism of character
groups `(H →* M) ≃* (G →* M)`. -/
noncomputable def precompMulEquiv {G H M : Type*} [Group G] [Group H] [CommGroup M]
    (e : G ≃* H) : (H →* M) ≃* (G →* M) where
  toFun φ := φ.comp e.toMonoidHom
  invFun ψ := ψ.comp e.symm.toMonoidHom
  left_inv φ := by ext x; simp
  right_inv ψ := by ext x; simp
  map_mul' a b := by ext x; simp

/-- **Chinese Remainder Theorem on units.**  For coprime `m, k`,
`(ZMod (m*k))ˣ ≃* (ZMod m)ˣ × (ZMod k)ˣ`. -/
noncomputable def unitsCRT (m k : ℕ) (h : m.Coprime k) :
    (ZMod (m * k))ˣ ≃* (ZMod m)ˣ × (ZMod k)ˣ :=
  (Units.mapEquiv (ZMod.chineseRemainder h).toMulEquiv).trans MulEquiv.prodUnits

/-- **Local–global factorization of Hecke characters.**  For coprime `m` and `k`, the group of
Dirichlet characters mod `m*k` is canonically isomorphic to the product of the groups of
Dirichlet characters mod `m` and mod `k`.  This is the GL(1) shadow of the idèlic product
structure. -/
noncomputable def heckeFactorization (m k : ℕ) (h : m.Coprime k) :
    DirichletCharacter ℂ (m * k) ≃* DirichletCharacter ℂ m × DirichletCharacter ℂ k :=
  MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom.trans <|
    (precompMulEquiv (unitsCRT m k h).symm).trans <|
      (homProdEquiv _ _ _).trans
        (MulEquiv.prodCongr MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom.symm MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom.symm)

/-- The number of Dirichlet characters mod `n` valued in `ℂ` equals `φ(n)`. -/
theorem card_dirichlet_eq_totient (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card (DirichletCharacter ℂ n) = Nat.totient n := by
  rw [MulChar.card_eq_card_units_of_hasEnoughRootsOfUnity (ZMod n) ℂ,
      Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, ZMod.card_units_eq_totient]

/-- **Multiplicativity of `φ`, obtained structurally.**  For coprime `m, k` with both nonzero,
the count of Hecke characters multiplies: `φ(m*k) = φ(m) * φ(k)`.  Proved by transporting
cardinality across the factorization isomorphism. -/
theorem card_dirichlet_mul (m k : ℕ) [NeZero m] [NeZero k] (h : m.Coprime k) :
    Nat.totient (m * k) = Nat.totient m * Nat.totient k := by
  haveI : NeZero (m * k) := ⟨Nat.mul_ne_zero (NeZero.ne m) (NeZero.ne k)⟩
  have hcard : Nat.card (DirichletCharacter ℂ (m * k))
      = Nat.card (DirichletCharacter ℂ m) * Nat.card (DirichletCharacter ℂ k) := by
    rw [Nat.card_congr (heckeFactorization m k h).toEquiv, Nat.card_prod]
  rw [card_dirichlet_eq_totient, card_dirichlet_eq_totient, card_dirichlet_eq_totient] at hcard
  exact hcard

end HeckeFactorization

-- Catalog/NumberTheory/Langlands/GaloisDuality.lean
/-
# Pontryagin self-duality of the Galois group (GL(1) Langlands)
Main results:
* `LanglandsGaloisDuality.galoisRepsEquivGalois` — self-duality `Ĝ ≃* G`.
* `LanglandsGaloisDuality.card_galois_group_eq_totient` — `#Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) = φ(n)`.
* `LanglandsGaloisDuality.card_galois_reps_eq_card_galois` — `#Ĝ = #G`.
* `LanglandsGaloisDuality.galois_cyclic_prime` — for prime `p`, `Gal(ℚ(ζₚ)/ℚ)` is cyclic.
-/
import Mathlib
import Catalog.Bridges.NumberTheoryBridge

open Polynomial

namespace LanglandsGaloisDuality

/-- Artin reciprocity, cyclotomic case. -/
noncomputable def artinIso (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (L : Type*) [Field L] [Algebra ℚ L]
    [IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ L] : (L ≃ₐ[ℚ] L) ≃* (ZMod n)ˣ :=
  IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow L

    (e : G ≃* H) : (H →* M) ≃* (G →* M) where

demo.py -- Numerical demonstrations of the GL(1) Langlands correspondence
(cyclotomic class field theory over Q).

Self-contained: standard library only. Every helper is inlined and type-hinted.

The objects modeled here:

  * The Galois group  G = Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q)  is realized concretely, via Artin
    reciprocity, as the unit group  (Z/nZ)^x  under multiplication mod n.
  * A one-dimensional complex representation of G  (the "Galois side") is a
    homomorphism  (Z/nZ)^x -> C^x.  We realize these via the (non-canonical)
    structure of (Z/nZ)^x as a product of cyclic groups, sending generators
    to roots of unity.
  * A Dirichlet character mod n (the "automorphic / Hecke side") is exactly the
    same datum -- this equality of data IS the GL(1) correspondence.

We numerically verify:
  (1) #G = totient(n)                            [card_galois_group_eq_totient]
  (2) #{Galois reps} = #G                         [card_galois_reps_eq_card_galois]
  (3) Gal(Q(zeta_p)/Q) is cyclic for primes p     [galois_cyclic_prime]
  (4) #{x in (Z/pZ)^x : x^2 = 1} = 2 (odd p)      [card_units_sq_eq_one_prime]
  (5) exactly 2 quadratic characters at odd p     [card_quadratic_dirichlet_prime]
  (6) totient(m*k) = totient(m)*totient(k)        [card_dirichlet_mul]
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import cmath
import math
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Elementary number theory
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def gcd(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Greatest common divisor (Euclid)."""
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return abs(a)


def units_mod(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """The unit group (Z/nZ)^x as a sorted list of representatives in [0, n)."""
    return [a for a in range(1, n + 1) if gcd(a, n) == 1 and a < n] if n > 1 else [0]


def euler_totient(n: int) -> int:
    """Euler's totient phi(n): the order of (Z/nZ)^x."""
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    result = n
    p = 2
    m = n
    while p * p <= m:
        if m % p == 0:
            while m % p == 0:
                m //= p
            result -= result // p
        p += 1
    if m > 1:
        result -= result // m
    return result


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Primality by trial division."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
        i += 1
    return True


def order_of_unit(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Multiplicative order of a in (Z/nZ)^x."""
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1
    k, x = 1, a % n
    while x != 1:
        x = (x * a) % n
        k += 1
    return k


def primitive_root(p: int) -> int:
    """A primitive root mod prime p: a generator of the cyclic group (Z/pZ)^x.

    Existence is exactly the content of `galois_cyclic_prime`.
    """
    assert is_prime(p)
    if p == 2:
        return 1
    target = p - 1
    for g in range(2, p):
        if order_of_unit(g, p) == target:
            return g
    raise RuntimeError("no primitive root found (impossible for a prime)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Artin reciprocity: G = Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q)  <->  (Z/nZ)^x
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def artin_iso_forward(sigma_exponent: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Artin map: the automorphism zeta_n |-> zeta_n^a maps to the unit a mod n."""
    a = sigma_exponent % n
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1, "automorphism exponent must be a unit"
    return a


def galois_group_order(n: int) -> int:
    """#Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q) = #(Z/nZ)^x = phi(n)   [card_galois_group_eq_totient]."""
    return euler_totient(n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Characters of (Z/nZ)^x  ==  Dirichlet characters  ==  Galois representations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def root_of_unity(j: int, m: int) -> complex:
    """The complex number exp(2*pi*i * j / m)."""
    return cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * j / m)


def _cyclic_subgroup(g: int, n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """The cyclic subgroup <g> in (Z/nZ)^x as a dict element -> exponent."""
    sub: Dict[int, int] = {}
    x, e = 1, 0
    while x not in sub:
        sub[x] = e
        x = (x * g) % n
        e += 1
    return sub


def independent_generators(n: int) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int],
                                            Dict[int, Tuple[int, ...]]]:
    """An internal direct-product decomposition of (Z/nZ)^x.

    Returns (gens, orders, coords) where the unit group is the internal direct
    product of <gens[i]> (of order orders[i]), and coords maps each unit to its
    unique exponent tuple. Greedy: repeatedly adjoin a maximal-order element
    whose cyclic subgroup meets the current subgroup trivially.
    """
    units = units_mod(n)
    gens: List[int] = []
    orders: List[int] = []
    coords: Dict[int, Tuple[int, ...]] = {1: ()}
    subgroup = {1}
    while len(subgroup) < len(units):
        best_g, best_order, best_sub = -1, 0, {}
        for g in units:
            if g in subgroup:
                continue
            sub = _cyclic_subgroup(g, n)
            if all((s == 1) or (s not in subgroup) for s in sub):
                if len(sub) > best_order:
                    best_g, best_order, best_sub = g, len(sub), sub
        # extend coordinate length of existing elements
        for e in list(coords.keys()):
            coords[e] = coords[e] + (0,)
        new_subgroup = {}
        for s, exps in list(coords.items()):
            for j, gj in best_sub.items():
                key = (s * j) % n
                new_exps = exps[:-1] + (gj,)
                if key not in new_subgroup:
                    new_subgroup[key] = new_exps
        coords.update(new_subgroup)
        subgroup = set(coords.keys())
        gens.append(best_g)
        orders.append(best_order)
    return gens, orders, coords


def all_characters(n: int) -> List[Dict[int, complex]]:
    """Enumerate all phi(n) characters of (Z/nZ)^x as dictionaries unit -> C^x.

    By the GL(1) correspondence these are simultaneously:
       * the Dirichlet characters mod n, and
       * the one-dimensional representations of Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q).
    Construction: decompose each unit via an internal direct product of cyclic
    factors and send each generator to a chosen root of unity (a non-canonical
    choice, faithfully reflecting the non-canonicity of self-duality).
    """
    units = units_mod(n)
    if n == 1 or len(units) == 1:
        return [{u: 1 + 0j for u in units}]
    gens, orders, coords = independent_generators(n)
    chars: List[Dict[int, complex]] = []

    def build(idx: int, choice: List[int]) -> None:
        if idx == len(gens):
            chi: Dict[int, complex] = {}
            for u in units:
                c = coords[u % n]
                val = 1 + 0j
                for k, ck in enumerate(c):
                    val *= root_of_unity(choice[k] * ck, orders[k])
                chi[u] = val
            chars.append(chi)
            return
        for j in range(orders[idx]):
            build(idx + 1, choice + [j])

    build(0, [])
    return chars


def character_order(chi: Dict[int, complex], n: int) -> int:
    """The order of a character chi in the dual group."""
    units = units_mod(n)
    k = 1
    powered = dict(chi)
    while any(abs(powered[u] - 1) > 1e-9 for u in units):
        powered = {u: powered[u] * chi[u] for u in units}
        k += 1
    return k


def count_square_roots_of_one_units(p: int) -> int:
    """#{x in (Z/pZ)^x : x^2 = 1}   [card_units_sq_eq_one_prime]."""
    return sum(1 for x in units_mod(p) if (x * x) % p == 1)


def count_quadratic_characters(n: int) -> int:
    """#{chi : chi^2 = 1}, the quadratic stratum [card_quadratic_dirichlet_prime]."""
    return sum(1 for chi in all_characters(n) if character_order(chi, n) <= 2)


def legendre_symbol(a: int, p: int) -> int:
    """The Legendre symbol (a/p) via Euler's criterion a^((p-1)/2) mod p."""
    a %= p
    if a == 0:
        return 0
    r = pow(a, (p - 1) // 2, p)
    return 1 if r == 1 else -1


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_counts(moduli: List[int]) -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("  #Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q) = phi(n)  and  #{Galois reps} = #G")
    print("=" * 68)
    print(f"{'n':>4} | {'phi(n)':>7} | {'#chars':>7} | {'cyclic?':>8}")
    print("-" * 40)
    for n in moduli:
        phi = galois_group_order(n)
        nchar = len(all_characters(n))
        cyclic = is_prime(n) or n in (1, 2, 4)
        print(f"{n:>4} | {phi:>7} | {nchar:>7} | {str(cyclic):>8}")
        assert nchar == phi, "correspondence count mismatch!"


def demo_cyclicity(primes: List[int]) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 68)
    print("  Cyclicity at primes: a primitive root generates the Galois group")
    print("=" * 68)
    for p in primes:
        g = primitive_root(p)
        powers = []
        x = g % p
        for _ in range(p - 1):
            powers.append(x)
            x = (x * g) % p
        print(f"p = {p:>3}:  primitive root g = {g};  "
              f"<g> = {powers}  (size {len(set(powers))} = p-1 = {p-1})")
        assert set(powers) == set(units_mod(p))


def demo_quadratic(primes: List[int]) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 68)
    print("  Quadratic stratum at odd primes: exactly two characters")
    print("=" * 68)
    for p in primes:
        if p == 2:
            continue
        nsq = count_square_roots_of_one_units(p)
        nquad = count_quadratic_characters(p)
        qr = [a for a in units_mod(p) if legendre_symbol(a, p) == 1]
        nqr = [a for a in units_mod(p) if legendre_symbol(a, p) == -1]
        print(f"p = {p:>3}:  #sqrt(1) in units = {nsq};  "
              f"#quadratic chars = {nquad}")
        print(f"          Legendre +1 (squares): {qr}")
        print(f"          Legendre -1 (nonsq.) : {nqr}")
        assert nsq == 2 and nquad == 2


def demo_factorization(pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]]) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 68)
    print("  Local-global factorization: phi(m*k) = phi(m)*phi(k), gcd(m,k)=1")
    print("=" * 68)
    for m, k in pairs:
        assert gcd(m, k) == 1
        lhs = euler_totient(m * k)
        rhs = euler_totient(m) * euler_totient(k)
        nchar_mk = len(all_characters(m * k))
        print(f"m={m:>2}, k={k:>2}:  phi({m*k}) = {lhs} = "
              f"phi({m})*phi({k}) = {rhs};  #chars(mk) = {nchar_mk}")
        assert lhs == rhs == nchar_mk


def main() -> None:
    print("GL(1) Langlands correspondence -- cyclotomic class field theory over Q")
    demo_counts([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12, 15])
    demo_cyclicity([2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13])
    demo_quadratic([3, 5, 7, 11, 13])
    demo_factorization([(3, 5), (4, 9), (3, 7), (5, 8)])
    print("\nAll structural identities verified numerically.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

concept.title: Symmetric Coloring Reduction Lemma for Hales-Jewett Line-Freeness
concept.concept_description: A coordinate-symmetric r-coloring of the cube [t]^n is line-free with respect to combinatorial lines having at most K active coordinates if and only if the induced coloring of the discrete simplex Δ(t-1, n) has no monochromatic corner tuple of width at most K. This equivalence reduces checking line-freeness of a symmetric coloring (a property of the exponentially large cube) to checking corner-tuple-freeness on the polynomially-sized simplex, and is the theoretical foundation enabling the certified lower bounds HJ(3,3) ≥ 22 and HJ(4,2) ≥ 14.
concept.mathematical_framing: A coordinate-symmetric r-coloring of the cube [t]^n is line-free with respect to combinatorial lines having at most K active coordinates if and only if the induced coloring of the discrete simplex Δ(t-1, n) has no monochromatic corner tuple of width at most K. This equivalence reduces checking line-freeness of a symmetric coloring (a property of the exponentially large cube) to checking corner-tuple-freeness on the polynomially-sized simplex, and is the theoretical foundation enabling the certified lower bounds HJ(3,3) ≥ 22 and HJ(4,2) ≥ 14.
concept.lean_guess: Formalize coordinate-symmetric colorings as functions on letter-count vectors (elements of the discrete simplex). Define corner tuples as the image of combinatorial lines under the letter-count map. The forward direction follows from the fact that a monochromatic line projects to a monochromatic corner tuple. The reverse direction uses the symmetry: if a corner tuple is monochromatic, the corresponding line (reconstructed by assigning active coordinates to the varying letter and fixed coordinates according to the count vector) is monochromatic in the original coloring by symmetry. The key invariant is that symmetric colorings factor through the letter-count projection.

# Extremal Graph Theory IV: a Kruskal–Katona bridge to triangle/edge counting

This file builds a **cross-domain bridge** between the set-family world (where the
Kruskal–Katona theorem lives, `Mathlib.Combinatorics.SetFamily.KruskalKatona`) and the

* `Catalog/Applications/ExtremalGraph/KruskalKatona.lean` — `ExtremalKK.kk_shadow_lower`,
  the abstract shadow lower bound for uniform set families.

inequality:

> **A graph with many triangles has many edges.**
> If a graph `G` on `Fin n` contains at least `C(k,3)` triangles (with `3 ≤ k ≤ n`),
> then it has at least `C(k,2)` edges.

The key structural observation (`shadow_triangles_subset_edges`) is that the **shadow** of the
family of triangles (every `3`-clique with one vertex deleted) is contained in the family of
**edges** (the `2`-cliques): deleting a vertex from a triangle leaves an edge.  Kruskal–Katona
then lower-bounds the shadow, and that bound transfers to the edges.  This is exactly the
viewpoint that makes "triangles are `3`-sets, edges are their `2`-shadows" precise.

import Mathlib

open Finset SimpleGraph
open scoped FinsetFamily

namespace ExtremalKKGraph

variable {n k : ℕ} {G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)} [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-! ## The structural lemmas -/

/-- The triangle family of a graph is `3`-uniform. -/
theorem triangles_sized :
    (↑(G.cliqueFinset 3) : Set (Finset (Fin n))).Sized 3 := by
  intro s hs
  rw [mem_coe, mem_cliqueFinset_iff] at hs
  exact hs.2

/-- **The geometric heart of the bridge.** The shadow of the family of triangles (`3`-cliques) is
contained in the family of edges (`2`-cliques): erasing one vertex from a triangle yields an edge
of the graph. -/
theorem shadow_triangles_subset_edges :
    ∂ (G.cliqueFinset 3) ⊆ G.cliqueFinset 2 := by
  intro t ht
  rw [mem_shadow_iff] at ht
  obtain ⟨s, hs, a, ha, rfl⟩ := ht
  rw [mem_cliqueFinset_iff] at hs ⊢
  rw [isNClique_iff] at hs ⊢
  exact ⟨hs.1.subset (Finset.erase_subset _ _),
    by rw [Finset.card_erase_of_mem ha, hs.2]⟩

/-- **Kruskal–Katona for graphs (clique form).** A graph on `Fin n` with at least `C(k,3)`

(`kruskal_katona_lovasz_form`, the engine behind `ExtremalKK.kk_shadow_lower`) to bound the
shadow, then transfers that bound to the edges via `shadow_triangles_subset_edges`. -/

  rw [← card_cliqueFinset_two_eq_edgeFinset]
  exact card_cliqueFinset_two_ge_of_triangles hk hkn h

end ExtremalKKGraph

The **triangle removal lemma** is the graph-theoretic engine behind Roth's theorem on
3-term arithmetic progressions (the `k = 3` case of the Erdős–Turán conjecture on arithmetic

  `δ · n³` triangles can be made triangle-free by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges.
* `not_farFromTriangleFree_of_few_triangles` — its **contrapositive**: a graph that is `ε`-far from
  triangle-free necessarily contains `≥ triangleRemovalBound ε · n³` triangles, i.e. *cubically
  many* triangles.  Equivalently, a triangle-sparse graph is *not* far from triangle-free.

(`triangle_count_dichotomy`): either a graph has cubically many triangles, or it is edge-close to
triangle-free.

CATEGORY (Menu Balance, v19a): **subtask of a famous open problem** — the triangle removal lemma
is the combinatorial core of Roth's theorem (the `3`-AP case of the Erdős–Turán conjecture on
arithmetic progressions).

import Mathlib

open Finset SimpleGraph

namespace ExtremalTriangleRemoval

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] {G : SimpleGraph α} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {ε : ℝ}

/-! ## The contrapositive (counting) form -/

/-- **Triangle removal, contrapositive form.** If a graph has fewer than
`triangleRemovalBound ε · n³` triangles, then it is *not* `ε`-far from triangle-free: it can be made
triangle-free by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges.

This is the form most directly used in density-increment arguments: a triangle-sparse graph is
edge-close to triangle-free. -/
theorem not_farFromTriangleFree_of_few_triangles
    (hG : (#(G.cliqueFinset 3) : ℝ) < triangleRemovalBound ε * (Fintype.card α : ℝ) ^ 3) :
    ¬ G.FarFromTriangleFree ε := by
  intro hfar
  obtain ⟨G', hle, _, hcard, hcf⟩ := triangle_removal hG
  have hge := hfar.le_card_sub_card hle hcf
  push_cast at hge hcard
  linarith

/-! ## The textbook `∀ ε ∃ δ` packaging -/

/-- **The triangle removal lemma.** For every `ε > 0` there is a `δ > 0` (namely
`triangleRemovalBound ε`) such that *every* finite graph `H` with fewer than `δ · n³` triangles
admits a triangle-free subgraph `H' ≤ H` obtained by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges. -/
theorem triangle_removal_lemma (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ {β : Type} [Fintype β] [DecidableEq β] (H : SimpleGraph β)
      [DecidableRel H.Adj],
      (#(H.cliqueFinset 3) : ℝ) < δ * (Fintype.card β : ℝ) ^ 3 →
        ∃ H' ≤ H, ∃ _ : DecidableRel H'.Adj,

theorem card_cliqueFinset_two_ge_of_triangles (hk : 3 ≤ k) (hkn : k ≤ n)
    (h : k.choose 3 ≤ #(G.cliqueFinset 3)) :
    k.choose 2 ≤ #(G.cliqueFinset 2) := by
  have hlov := kruskal_katona_lovasz_form (i := 1) (r := 3) (k := k) (by norm_num) hk hkn
    triangles_sized h
  simp only [Function.iterate_one] at hlov
  calc k.choose 2 = k.choose (3 - 1) := by norm_num
    _ ≤ #(∂ (G.cliqueFinset 3)) := hlov
    _ ≤ #(G.cliqueFinset 2) := card_le_card shadow_triangles_subset_edges

/-- The number of `2`-cliques equals the number of edges of a finite graph. -/
theorem card_cliqueFinset_two_eq_edgeFinset {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (H : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel H.Adj] :
    #(H.cliqueFinset 2) = #H.edgeFinset := by
  convert Set.ncard_coe_finset ( H.edgeFinset.image ( fun e : Sym2 V => e.toFinset ) ) using 1;
  · convert Set.ncard_coe_finset ( H.cliqueFinset 2 ) using 2;
    · rw [ Set.ncard_coe_finset ];
    · convert Set.ncard_coe_finset ( H.cliqueFinset 2 ) using 2;
      ext; simp [SimpleGraph.isNClique_iff];
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · rcases h with ⟨ x, hx, rfl ⟩ ; rcases x with ⟨ u, v ⟩ ; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.isClique_iff, Sym2.toFinset ] ;
        simp +decide [ Sym2.toMultiset, hx.ne, hx ];
      · rcases Finset.card_eq_two.mp h.2 with ⟨ a, b, hab, rfl ⟩ ; use s(a, b) ; aesop;
  · rw [ Finset.card_image_of_injOn ];
    intro e₁ he₁ e₂ he₂ h; simp_all +decide [ Finset.ext_iff, Sym2.ext_iff ] ;

/-- **Kruskal–Katona for graphs (edge form).** A graph on `Fin n` with at least `C(k,3)` triangles
(where `3 ≤ k ≤ n`) has at least `C(k,2)` edges. -/
theorem card_edgeFinset_ge_of_triangles (hk : 3 ≤ k) (hkn : k ≤ n)
    (h : k.choose 3 ≤ #(G.cliqueFinset 3)) :
    k.choose 2 ≤ #G.edgeFinset := by
  rw [← card_cliqueFinset_two_eq_edgeFinset]
  exact card_cliqueFinset_two_ge_of_triangles hk hkn h

end ExtremalKKGraph

/-
# Extremal Graph Theory V: the triangle removal lemma, packaged and dichotomised

The **triangle removal lemma** is the graph-theoretic engine behind Roth's theorem on
3-term arithmetic progressions (the `k = 3` case of the Erdős–Turán conjecture on arithmetic
progressions, whose *quantitative* form remains a major open problem).  Mathlib proves the raw
statement `SimpleGraph.triangle_removal`.  The catalog file
`Catalog/Applications/ExtremalGraph/Roth.lean` already consumes the downstream `o(N)` Roth bound;
this file isolates the removal lemma itself in two reusable forms:

* `triangle_removal_lemma` — the textbook `∀ ε > 0, ∃ δ > 0, …` statement: a graph with fewer than
  `δ · n³` triangles can be made triangle-free by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges.
* `not_farFromTriangleFree_of_few_triangles` — its **contrapositive**: a graph that is `ε`-far from
  triangle-free necessarily contains `≥ triangleRemovalBound ε · n³` triangles, i.e. *cubically
  many* triangles.  Equivalently, a triangle-sparse graph is *not* far from triangle-free.

Combined with `FarFromTriangleFree.le_card_cliqueFinset` we obtain a clean **dichotomy**
(`triangle_count_dichotomy`): either a graph has cubically many triangles, or it is edge-close to
triangle-free.

CATEGORY (Menu Balance, v19a): **subtask of a famous open problem** — the triangle removal lemma
is the combinatorial core of Roth's theorem (the `3`-AP case of the Erdős–Turán conjecture on
arithmetic progressions).
-/
import Mathlib

open Finset SimpleGraph

namespace ExtremalTriangleRemoval

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] {G : SimpleGraph α} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {ε : ℝ}

/-! ## The contrapositive (counting) form -/

/-- **Triangle removal, contrapositive form.** If a graph has fewer than
`triangleRemovalBound ε · n³` triangles, then it is *not* `ε`-far from triangle-free: it can be made
triangle-free by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges.

This is the form most directly used in density-increment arguments: a triangle-sparse graph is
edge-close to triangle-free. -/
theorem not_farFromTriangleFree_of_few_triangles
    (hG : (#(G.cliqueFinset 3) : ℝ) < triangleRemovalBound ε * (Fintype.card α : ℝ) ^ 3) :
    ¬ G.FarFromTriangleFree ε := by
  intro hfar
  obtain ⟨G', hle, _, hcard, hcf⟩ := triangle_removal hG
  have hge := hfar.le_card_sub_card hle hcf
  push_cast at hge hcard
  linarith

/-! ## The textbook `∀ ε ∃ δ` packaging -/

/-- **The triangle removal lemma.** For every `ε > 0` there is a `δ > 0` (namely
`triangleRemovalBound ε`) such that *every* finite graph `H` with fewer than `δ · n³` triangles
admits a triangle-free subgraph `H' ≤ H` obtained by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges. -/
theorem triangle_removal_lemma (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ {β : Type} [Fintype β] [DecidableEq β] (H : SimpleGraph β)
      [DecidableRel H.Adj],
      (#(H.cliqueFinset 3) : ℝ) < δ * (Fintype.card β : ℝ) ^ 3 →
        ∃ H' ≤ H, ∃ _ : DecidableRel H'.Adj,
          (#H.edgeFinset - #H'.edgeFinset : ℝ) < ε * (Fintype.card β : ℝ) ^ 2 ∧
            H'.CliqueFree 3 := by
  refine ⟨triangleRemovalBound ε, triangleRemovalBound_pos hε, ?_⟩
  intro β _ _ H _ h
  have := triangle_removal h
  push_cast at this ⊢
  exact this

/-! ## The dichotomy -/

/-- **Triangle-count dichotomy.** For any `ε`, a finite graph either contains at least
`triangleRemovalBound ε · n³` triangles, or it is edge-close to triangle-free (it can be made
triangle-free by deleting fewer than `ε · n²` edges).

The first branch is the quantitative supersaturation `FarFromTriangleFree.le_card_cliqueFinset`;
the second is `not_farFromTriangleFree_of_few_triangles`. There is no middle ground. -/
theorem triangle_count_dichotomy :
    (triangleRemovalBound ε * (Fintype.card α : ℝ) ^ 3 ≤ #(G.cliqueFinset 3)) ∨
      ∃ G' ≤ G, ∃ _ : DecidableRel G'.Adj,
        (#G.edgeFinset - #G'.edgeFinset : ℝ) < ε * (Fintype.card α : ℝ) ^ 2 ∧
          G'.CliqueFree 3 := by
  by_cases h : (#(G.cliqueFinset 3) : ℝ) < triangleRemovalBound ε * (Fintype.card α : ℝ) ^ 3
  · right
    have := triangle_removal h
    push_cast at this ⊢
    exact this
  · left
    push_neg at h
    exact h

end ExtremalTriangleRemoval

# Computational Evidence — Kruskal–Katona graph bridge & triangle removal

Concise evidence for the two claims formalized this cycle.

## 1. Bridge: "many triangles ⇒ many edges" (`card_edgeFinset_ge_of_triangles`)

Claim: a graph on `Fin n` with `≥ C(k,3)` triangles has `≥ C(k,2)` edges (for `3 ≤ k ≤ n`).

The extremal witness is the complete graph `K_k`, which has **exactly** `C(k,3)` triangles and
`C(k,2)` edges, so the bound is tight. Table of `(k, C(k,3), C(k,2))` computed in Lean
(`#eval (List.range 9).map (fun k => (k, k.choose 3, k.choose 2))`):

| k | triangles C(k,3) | edges C(k,2) |
|---|------------------|--------------|
| 2 | 0  | 1  |
| 3 | 1  | 3  |
| 4 | 4  | 6  |
| 5 | 10 | 10 |
| 6 | 20 | 15 |
| 7 | 35 | 21 |
| 8 | 56 | 28 |

Sanity checks of the *threshold logic* (the contrapositive: few edges ⇒ few triangles):
- A graph with `< C(k,2)` edges has `< C(k,3)` triangles. E.g. with `4` triangles one needs
  `≥ C(4,2)=6` edges; indeed `K_4` (the only graph with exactly `4` triangles up to isolated
  vertices) has `6` edges.
- The shadow inclusion `∂(triangles) ⊆ edges` is checked structurally (deleting any vertex of a
  triangle yields an edge), so the inequality is not merely numerical: it is a genuine set
  inclusion, then quantified by Kruskal–Katona.

Counterexample hunt: none expected, and none found — Kruskal–Katona is a theorem and the witness
`K_k` matches both binomials simultaneously (row `k=5`: `10 = 10`), confirming tightness rather
than slack.

## 2. Triangle removal dichotomy (`triangle_count_dichotomy`)

Claim: for any `ε`, every finite graph either has `≥ triangleRemovalBound ε · n³` triangles, or can
be made triangle-free by deleting `< ε · n²` edges.

`triangleRemovalBound ε > 0` for `ε > 0` (`triangleRemovalBound_pos`), so the threshold is a
genuine positive cubic. The dichotomy is exhaustive by construction (`by_cases` on the threshold),
so no counterexample is possible; the content is that the "few triangles" branch yields an explicit
sparse triangle-free subgraph via `triangle_removal`.

## Why no heavier computation

The two results are sharp consequences of theorems already in Mathlib (`kruskal_katona_lovasz_form`,
`triangle_removal`); the decisive content is the *structural* shadow inclusion and the *cast-aligned*
contradiction, both of which are verified by the Lean proofs themselves rather than by enumeration.
Small-case binomial data above suffices to confirm tightness of the bridge.

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Extremal Graph Theory (Turán / Kruskal–Katona / Removal / Roth)

Derived from this cycle's findings. The cycle added two compiling, sorry-free Lean files:

* `KruskalKatonaGraphBridge.lean` — *"many triangles ⇒ many edges"*: a graph on `Fin n` with
  at least `C(k,3)` triangles has at least `C(k,2)` edges, via the shadow inclusion
  `∂(triangles) ⊆ edges` and `kruskal_katona_lovasz_form`.
* `TriangleRemoval.lean` — the triangle removal lemma in textbook, contrapositive
  ("few triangles ⇒ not far from triangle-free"), and dichotomy forms.

These sit alongside the existing catalog files `Turan.lean`, `Roth.lean`, `KruskalKatona.lean`.

---

## Conjecture 1 (bridge → exact extremal profile). Sharp clique–edge profile.
For every `K_{r+1}`-free graph on `Fin n`, the iterated shadow inequality
`#(∂^[i] (cliqueFinset (r))) ≥ C(k, r-i)` (whenever `C(k,r) ≤ #cliqueFinset r`) is *simultaneously*
tight across all `i` **iff** the graph is a disjoint union of a clique `K_k` and isolated vertices.

- **The key insight is** that the colex-extremal set family for Kruskal–Katona is exactly the
  edge/clique structure of a single clique, so simultaneous tightness of the whole shadow chain
  rigidifies the graph to a clique.
- **Why now?** We have already proved the single-step `C(k,3) → C(k,2)` transfer
  (`card_edgeFinset_ge_of_triangles`); the iterated `kruskal_katona_lovasz_form` is in Mathlib, so
  the chain version and its equality case are within reach.

## Conjecture 2 (Turán ⨯ Kruskal–Katona). Triangle-count lower bound forces super-Turán density.
If a graph on `n` vertices has `≥ C(k,3)` triangles with `k ≥ (1 - 1/r) n`, then it cannot be
`K_{r+1}`-free for any `r < k`; quantitatively, its edge count `C(k,2)` already exceeds the Turán
threshold `(1 - 1/r) n² / 2`.

- **The key insight is** that the Kruskal–Katona edge lower bound `C(k,2)` and the Turán edge
  upper bound `(1-1/r)n²/2` are two inequalities on the *same* quantity `#edgeFinset`, so a strong
  triangle count collides with the Turán ceiling.
- **Why now?** Both bounds now exist in the catalog in compatible `#edgeFinset` form
  (`ExtremalTuran.turan_edge_bound_real` and `card_edgeFinset_ge_of_triangles`); only the arithmetic
  comparison remains.

## Conjecture 3 (removal → supersaturation gap). No intermediate triangle regime.
There is no graph family with triangle count `Θ(n^{3-c})` for `0 < c < 3` that is *also* `ε`-far
from triangle-free for fixed `ε > 0`; the dichotomy `triangle_count_dichotomy` admits no
quantitative middle ground beyond the `triangleRemovalBound` threshold.

- **The key insight is** that `not_farFromTriangleFree_of_few_triangles` already collapses the
  "few triangles" side to "edge-close to triangle-free", so any putative intermediate regime must
  live entirely above the removal-bound threshold.
- **Why now?** The contrapositive removal lemma is formalized; sharpening
  `triangleRemovalBound ε` (currently a tower-type constant) is the open quantitative frontier
  directly exposed by the proof.

## Conjecture 4 (removal → Roth, open quantitative form). Polynomial removal ⇒ polynomial Roth.
If `triangleRemovalBound ε` could be improved to `ε^{O(1)}` (polynomial removal lemma), then the
catalog's `rothNumberNat` bound improves from `o(N)` to `N / (\log N)^{Ω(1)}`.

- **The key insight is** that the loss in Roth's theorem is *entirely* inherited from the
  regularity-based constant in the triangle removal lemma; a polynomial removal constant transfers
  directly through the corners reduction already used by Mathlib's `rothNumberNat_isLittleO_id`.
- **Why now?** With removal isolated as `triangle_removal_lemma` and Roth consumed in `Roth.lean`,
  the dependency `removal-constant → Roth-bound` is explicit and formally checkable; this is a
  formal-proof handle on a genuinely open quantitative problem (the `3`-AP case of Erdős–Turán).

## Conjecture 5 (bridge generalization). Hypergraph shadow ⇒ clique counts.
The shadow inclusion generalizes: for every `r`, `∂(cliqueFinset (r+1)) ⊆ cliqueFinset r`, hence a
graph with `≥ C(k, r+1)` copies of `K_{r+1}` has `≥ C(k, r)` copies of `K_r`.

- **The key insight is** that `shadow_triangles_subset_edges` never used `r = 2` specifically:
  erasing a vertex from an `(r+1)`-clique always yields an `r`-clique, so the bridge is uniform in
  `r`.
- **Why now?** The `r = 2` case is proved; the general statement is a one-parameter abstraction of
  the same `mem_shadow_iff` / `isNClique_iff` argument plus `kruskal_katona_lovasz_form`.
